pos: n. (the capital of Silesia on the Oder, now Wroclaw; a Lutheran city under a Catholic bishop for three centuries)
etymology: From the Slavic personal name Vratislav, germanised Breslau; the Polish Wroclaw preserves the older form.
biblical_def: Breslau was the chief city of Silesia and the seat of its bishop. The council called Johann Hess to St Mary Magdalene in 1523, held a public disputation in 1524, and carried the city over to the Reformation within a few years, while the bishop and his cathedral chapter remained Catholic and stayed where they were. The result was one of the longest-running arrangements of its kind in Europe: a Lutheran city with Lutheran parish churches, a Lutheran school and a Lutheran press, governing itself around a Catholic cathedral precinct it could not touch, under Habsburg sovereigns who were the leading Catholic power on the continent. It lasted, with pressure and interruption, until Prussia took Silesia in 1741. The dictionary records the city because the word made its way there by preaching in a town the gospel did not politically control: “So mightily grew the word of God and prevailed” (Act 19:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to prevail as to overcome, to gain the victory or superiority; a chapter as an assembly of the clergy of a cathedral; and a precinct as a district within certain boundaries.
webster_full: PREVAIL, v.i. [L. praevaleo.] To overcome; to gain the victory or superiority; to be in force; to have effect.
CHAPTER, n. [L. capitulum.] A society of clergymen belonging to a cathedral or collegiate church; the body of canons.
PRECINCT, n. [L. praecinctus.] The limit, bound or exterior line encompassing a place; a district within certain boundaries.
RICHLY, adv. With riches; with abundance; plenteously; truly; abundantly.
ADMONISH, v.t. [L. admoneo.] To warn or notify of a fault; to reprove with mildness; to counsel against wrong practices.
scriptures: So mightily grew the word of God and prevailed.
And the next sabbath day came almost the whole city together to hear the word of God.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Therefore many of them believed; also of honourable women which were Greeks, and of men, not a few.
corruption_summary: The Silesian capital on the Oder, now Wroclaw; Lutheran by council decision in the 1520s while its bishop and cathedral chapter remained Catholic until Prussia annexed Silesia in 1741.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Breslau is nevertheless a standing rebuke to a view held in every century, that the gospel cannot flourish where it does not hold the levers. The Breslau Lutherans had no sovereign of their own confession, a Catholic bishop inside their walls, and a Habsburg emperor over their heads who spent the seventeenth century dismantling Protestantism elsewhere in Silesia. What they had was preaching, a school, a press and a council that would not budge, and with those they kept a Lutheran city for two hundred years.

The principle to recover is that the word grows by its own power, and that its growth is reported as the word's achievement rather than the church's. Luke credits neither strategy nor patronage: “So mightily grew the word of God and prevailed” (Act 19:20). The means is the public hearing of it, with a whole city turning out — “And the next sabbath day came almost the whole city together to hear the word of God” (Act 13:44). And the way it is kept in a place is by lodging it in the people: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom” (Col 3:16).

pos: n. (1490–1547; reformer of Breslau and of Silesia, pastor of St Mary Magdalene for twenty-four years)
etymology: Hess, a German surname meaning a Hessian, a man of Hesse; Johann from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious.
biblical_def: Johann Hess was born at Nuremberg, studied at Leipzig and Wittenberg, served Bishop Johann Turzo of Breslau as secretary, travelled in Italy, and corresponded with Erasmus before Luther persuaded him. In 1523 the Breslau council called him to St Mary Magdalene over the chapter's objection. On 20 April 1524 he held a public disputation in the city — the first in Silesia — defending justification by faith and the sufficiency of Scripture, which effectively settled the matter for Breslau. He then spent twenty-four years as its chief pastor: church order, school, poor relief, visitation, and a steady refusal to be drawn either into Schwenckfeld's spiritualism on one side or into the sacramentarian quarrel on the other. The dictionary records him for the thoroughness Paul claims in his own farewell: “For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to shun as to avoid, to keep clear of; counsel as advice, deliberation, in Scripture the purpose and design of God; and a steward as one entrusted with the management of another's affairs.
webster_full: SHUN, v.t. [Saxon scunian.] To avoid; to keep clear of; to refuse to meddle with; to neglect purposely.
COUNSEL, n. [L. consilium.] Advice; deliberation; in a scriptural sense, the purpose, design and will of God.
STEWARD, n. A man employed to manage the affairs of another; one entrusted with what belongs to his master.
MYSTERY, n. [Gr. musterion.] A profound secret; in Scripture, something hidden which God has revealed.
PROFITABLE, a. Yielding or bringing profit or gain; gainful; useful; advantageous.

And how I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you, but have shewed you, and have taught you publickly, and from house to house,
Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God.
Jer 1:7
But the LORD said unto me, Say not, I am a child: for thou shalt go to all that I shall send thee, and whatsoever I command thee thou shalt speak.
corruption_summary: Reformer of Breslau: called to St Mary Magdalene in 1523, held Silesia's first public disputation in April 1524, and served as the city's chief pastor until 1547.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Hess is instead a correction to a false choice the Reformation's own historians sometimes offer: that a reformer was either a fighter or a moderate. Hess fought a public disputation that decided a province and then spent twenty-four years declining two fights — Schwenckfeld's and the sacramentarians' — because neither was his congregation's business. Discernment about which battle belongs to a pulpit is not timidity, and the pastor who fights every available controversy is not thereby braver.

The principle to recover is that a minister owes his people the whole counsel of God, and that the measure is completeness rather than intensity. Paul's defence of his ministry is an inventory: nothing withheld, taught publicly and privately, “And how I kept back nothing that was profitable unto you, but have shewed you, and have taught you publickly, and from house to house” (Act 20:20), summed up as “For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27). What he is, he says, is a trustee of something not his own — “stewards of the mysteries of God” (1Co 4:1) — and a man who pleads unfitness is answered as Jeremiah was (Jer 1:7).

pos: n. (1494–1554; pastor of St Elizabeth's in Breslau and author of the Silesian catechism of 1535)
etymology: Moibanus, a latinised form of the Silesian surname Moiban; Ambrosius, from Greek ambrosios, immortal.
biblical_def: Ambrosius Moibanus was a Breslau man, studied at Vienna and Wittenberg where he took his doctorate in 1525, and from that year was pastor of St Elizabeth's, the city's other great parish, until he died in 1554. He worked alongside Hess for nearly thirty years and was the more gifted catechist of the two. His Catechismi capita decem of 1535, a ten-part catechism with hymns and prayers, was the instrument by which Silesia's children were actually taught, and he wrote a book of family devotions and several hymns besides. He also pressed the council hard on poor relief and on the schools, and on the examination of candidates for the ministry. The dictionary records him because catechising is the Lord's own priority about children and not a lesser kind of ministry: “Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not” (Mar 10:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a catechist as one who instructs by question and answer, particularly in religion; a precept as a commandment or rule of moral conduct; and milk as a liquid secreted for the nourishment of young, figuratively elementary doctrine.
webster_full: CATECHIST, n. One who instructs by question and answer; one appointed to instruct catechumens in the principles of religion.
PRECEPT, n. [L. praeceptum.] Any commandment or order intended as an authoritative rule of action; a maxim; a rule of moral conduct.
MILK, n. A white fluid secreted by females for the nourishment of their young; figuratively, the first elements of doctrine.
PRINCIPLE, n. [L. principium.] Element; the first elementary parts of a body or of a subject; a ground of action.
SUFFER, v.t. To allow; to permit; to not forbid or hinder; to bear, to endure.
scriptures: But when Jesus saw it, he was much displeased, and said unto them, Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God.
For precept must be upon precept, precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here a little, and there a little:
Heb 5:12

For when for the time ye ought to be teachers, ye have need that one teach you again which be the first principles of the oracles of God; and are become such as have need of milk, and not of strong meat.
Heb 6:1
Therefore leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God,
corruption_summary: Pastor of St Elizabeth's in Breslau from 1525 to 1554 and author of the 1535 catechism by which Silesia's children were taught.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error worth naming is one every church is tempted to: treating catechesis as the junior department, the thing assigned to whoever is not needed in the pulpit. Breslau did the opposite. Its second great parish was held for thirty years by the man who wrote the catechism, and the catechism, not the sermons, is what shaped the next generation of Silesians. A church that hands its children to its least-regarded workers has made a decision about its future whether it means to or not.

The principle to recover is that children are to be brought and not fended off, and that elementary teaching is a real foundation rather than a holding pattern. Mark records that the Lord was much displeased at the hindering, and the command he gave is unqualified: “Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God” (Mar 10:14). The method is slow and repetitive by design — “For precept must be upon precept, precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here a little, and there a little” (Isa 28:10). Hebrews rebukes those who need the milk again when they should be teaching (Heb 5:12), and then presses on from the foundation rather than demolishing it (Heb 6:1).

pos: n. (1480–1547; Duke of Legnica and Brieg, the first prince to establish the Reformation in Silesia)
etymology: Frederick, from Old High German fridu, peace, and rihhi, rule; a name meaning peaceful ruler.
biblical_def: Frederick II was Duke of Legnica from 1488 and of Brieg from 1521, a Piast prince of the old Silesian line. He took up the Reformation early, by 1522 and formally in 1524, and was the first ruler in Silesia to establish it in his duchies — appointing evangelical preachers, ordering visitations, dissolving monasteries, and in 1526 founding at Liegnitz a university on the Wittenberg pattern. That foundation collapsed within three years, partly because the duke had also become Caspar Schwenckfeld's patron and the school took on the spiritualist colouring that followed Schwenckfeld everywhere. Frederick later distanced himself and Schwenckfeld left Silesia for good in 1529. The dictionary records him for the thing he did well and for the model: Jehoshaphat sent teachers through his own towns with the book in their hands. “And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them” (2Ch 17:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a duke as a sovereign prince, the ruler of a duchy; mercy as that benevolence which disposes to overlook injuries; and to uphold as to support, to sustain, to keep from falling.
webster_full: DUKE, n. [L. dux, a leader.] A sovereign prince, ruler of a state called a duchy; a nobleman of the highest order.
MERCY, n. That benevolence, mildness or tenderness of heart which disposes a person to overlook injuries, or to treat an offender better than he deserves.
UPHOLD, v.t. To support; to sustain; to keep from falling or declining; to maintain.
VISITATION, n. The official visit of a superior to a church or district for inspection and correction.
STATUTE, n. [L. statutum.] An act of the legislature; a law; a special law or ordinance.
scriptures: And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them, and went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people.
Also in the third year of his reign he sent to his princes, even to Benhail, and to Obadiah, and to Zechariah, and to Nethaneel, and to Michaiah, to teach in the cities of Judah.
And it shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the LORD his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them:
Mercy and truth preserve the king: and his throne is upholden by mercy.
corruption_summary: Duke of Legnica and Brieg, the first Silesian prince to establish the Reformation, who founded a university at Liegnitz in 1526 and was for a time Schwenckfeld's patron.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Frederick's entry has to hold a real failure alongside a real achievement. He was first in Silesia, and first is worth something. He also gave Schwenckfeld a court, a hearing and a university, and Schwenckfeld's doctrine of the celestial flesh of Christ and his disparagement of the sacraments and of the external word spread from Legnica outward and troubled Silesian Lutheranism for a century. A prince who protects a teacher before he has weighed the teaching has used his office to amplify something he does not understand.

The principle to recover is the shape of Jehoshaphat's reform, which is the Bible's own picture of a godly ruler and has two features worth marking. He sent men out rather than summoning people in, and the five princes are named one by one before their errand is stated: “to teach in the cities of Judah” (2Ch 17:7). And what the teachers carried was not the duke's programme but a text: “And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them” (2Ch 17:9). The king himself is to read it all his life (Deu 17:19), and his throne is upheld by mercy rather than by his patronage of clever men (Pro 20:28).

pos: n. (the Silesian ducal town, now Legnica; the first place in Silesia to be reformed and the site of a short-lived university)
etymology: From the Slavic Legnica, possibly from leg, a low-lying place, germanised Liegnitz.
biblical_def: Liegnitz was the seat of the Piast dukes of Legnica, and under Frederick II it became in 1522 the first town in Silesia where the Reformation was established by its ruler. In 1526 Frederick founded a university there, the Academia, meant to be a Wittenberg for the Silesian lands, with Valentin Krautwald and Schwenckfeld's circle prominent in it. It failed within three years: the Schwenckfeldian colouring made it suspect to Lutherans and Catholics alike, Frederick lost confidence, and the project was abandoned by 1530. Silesia would have no university until Breslau's Leopoldina in 1702, a Jesuit foundation. Liegnitz remained Lutheran and Piast until the line died out in 1675. The dictionary records the town because a failed school still teaches what a school is for: “Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding” (Pro 4:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an academy as a school or seminary of learning; a defence as that which guards or protects, a shelter; and inspiration as the infusion of ideas into the mind by the Holy Spirit.
webster_full: ACADEMY, n. [Gr. akademia.] A school or seminary of learning, holding a rank between a university and a common school; a society of learned men.
DEFENCE, n. [L. defendo.] Any thing that opposes attack, violence or injury; protection; guard; vindication.
INSPIRATION, n. The infusion of ideas into the mind by the Holy Spirit; the conveying into the minds of men ideas by extraordinary or supernatural influence.
PRINCIPAL, a. [L. principalis.] Chief; highest in rank, authority or importance; most considerable.
INSTRUCTION, n. The act of teaching; information; precepts conveying knowledge.
scriptures: Pro 4:7
Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.
Ecc 7:12
For wisdom is a defence, and money is a defence: but the excellency of knowledge is, that wisdom giveth life to them that have it.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Come, ye children, hearken unto me: I will teach you the fear of the LORD.
corruption_summary: The Silesian ducal town, now Legnica, where Frederick II established the Reformation in 1522 and founded a university in 1526 that collapsed within three years.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson Liegnitz actually carries is one the modern church needs rather than one it has distorted. A university founded with a prince's money, in a good cause, at the right moment, failed because of who was allowed to teach in it. Doctrine was not a side matter of faculty appointments; it was the thing that decided whether the institution could exist. A school that will not say what it believes cannot be defended by anyone, and Liegnitz was not.

The principle to recover is that wisdom is to be sought as the chief acquisition and that it is a protection rather than an ornament. Proverbs makes it the priority over everything else a man accumulates: “Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding” (Pro 4:7). Ecclesiastes compares it to money and gives it the advantage — “but the excellency of knowledge is, that wisdom giveth life to them that have it” (Ecc 7:12). The curriculum has a given text, profitable for doctrine, reproof, correction and instruction (2Ti 3:16), and its first lesson is the fear of the LORD taught to children (Psa 34:11).

pos: n. (the Silesian Piast residence on the Oder, now Brzeg; seat of a Protestant gymnasium for a century and a half)
etymology: From Polish Brzeg, a bank or shore, germanised Brieg; the town on the river bank.
biblical_def: Brieg stands on the Oder below Breslau and was, with Liegnitz, the residence of the last Piast dukes. Frederick II held both duchies and reformed both; his successors kept the duchy Lutheran, rebuilt the castle in the Renaissance manner, and in 1569 founded the Gymnasium Illustre, which taught Silesian Protestants until the Piast line died out in 1675 and the Habsburgs took the duchy into direct rule. Brieg was the one place in Silesia where a Protestant prince, a Protestant school and a Protestant church held together without interruption for a hundred and fifty years, and generations of Silesian pastors were trained there. The dictionary records it as a plain instance of generational transmission done deliberately and over a long time: “One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts” (Psa 145:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a gymnasium as a place of exercise, in Germany a school of the higher kind; a generation as a single succession of men in natural descent; and to declare as to make known, to tell explicitly.
webster_full: GYMNASIUM, n. [Gr. gumnasion.] A place of exercise; in Germany, a school or seminary of the higher kind, preparatory to a university.
GENERATION, n. [L. generatio.] A single succession of men or animals in natural descent; the people of the same period.
DECLARE, v.t. [L. declaro.] To make known; to tell explicitly; to manifest or communicate plainly by words.
RESIDENCE, n. The act of abiding or dwelling in a place; the place of abode, especially of a prince.
HITHERTO, adv. To this time; yet; up to the present period.
scriptures: One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts.
O God, thou hast taught me from my youth: and hitherto have I declared thy wondrous works.
Deu 6:6
And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart:
Joe 1:3
Tell ye your children of it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation.
corruption_summary: The Silesian Piast residence on the Oder, now Brzeg, Lutheran from the 1520s, with a Protestant gymnasium founded in 1569 that lasted until the line died out in 1675.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Brieg does expose how fragile such an arrangement is, and the dictionary says so rather than presenting a hundred and fifty years as a success story with no conditions. The whole thing rested on a dynasty. When the last Piast duke died childless in 1675, the duchy passed to the Habsburgs and the Protestant establishment was dismantled by the ordinary operation of inheritance law. A church whose continuance depends on who a prince marries has built on something it does not control.

The principle to recover is that transmission between generations is a stated duty with a stated content, and that schools are one way of discharging it. The Psalm describes the handover as praise passed down a line: “One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts” (Psa 145:4). The individual testimony runs the same direction — “O God, thou hast taught me from my youth: and hitherto have I declared thy wondrous works” (Psa 71:17). Moses locates the words in the heart before the schoolroom (Deu 6:6), and Joel stretches the chain to four generations in one verse (Joe 1:3).

pos: n. (the Silesian duchy and town, now Olesnica; a Lutheran principality with a notable school and library)
etymology: From Polish Olesnica, from olcha, an alder, the place of alders; germanised Oels.
biblical_def: Oels was a small Silesian duchy north-east of Breslau, Lutheran from the Reformation and held from 1649 by the dukes of Wurttemberg-Oels, who ran it as a confessional Lutheran state within the Catholic Habsburg monarchy. Its gymnasium and its ducal library made it a quiet centre of Silesian Protestant learning, and its presses turned out devotional and school books for the whole region. The duchy was consistently the beneficiary of its own insignificance: too small to be worth the trouble of forcible re-Catholicisation, and so a refuge for men and books that were not safe elsewhere in Silesia. The dictionary records it because an unglamorous library in a small place is a real service to the church, and because Scripture is realistic about both the value and the limits of reading. “Apply thine heart unto instruction, and thine ears to the words of knowledge” (Pro 23:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a library as a collection of books belonging to a private person or to the public; prudent as cautious, circumspect, practically wise; and study as application of mind to books and learning.
webster_full: LIBRARY, n. [L. librarium.] A collection of books belonging to a private person, or to a public institution or a company.
PRUDENT, a. [L. prudens.] Cautious; circumspect; practically wise; careful of the consequences of enterprises.
STUDY, n. [L. studium.] Application of mind to books, to arts or science, or to any subject, for the purpose of learning.
WEARINESS, n. The state of being tired; lassitude; fatigue of body or of mind.
MEDITATE, v.i. [L. meditor.] To dwell on any thing in thought; to contemplate; to revolve in the mind.
scriptures: Apply thine heart unto instruction, and thine ears to the words of knowledge.
The heart of the prudent getteth knowledge; and the ear of the wise seeketh knowledge.
And further, by these, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
Psa 1:2
But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.
corruption_summary: A small Lutheran duchy north-east of Breslau, now Olesnica, held by the dukes of Wurttemberg-Oels from 1649, with a gymnasium, a ducal library and its own presses.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The temptation attached to a place like Oels is bibliolatry of the wrong kind: the confusion of a well-stocked library with a healthy church. Silesian Protestantism in the seventeenth century produced a great deal of print, some of it excellent and some of it the learned repetition of men who had stopped expecting anything from God. A duchy can own every book in the catalogue and still have a dead pulpit, and the dictionary will not pretend the shelves settle the question.

The principle to recover is that study is commanded and is also bounded. Proverbs puts the effort on the learner's side, as an act of the will: “Apply thine heart unto instruction, and thine ears to the words of knowledge” (Pro 23:12), and marks the appetite as the mark of wisdom — “the ear of the wise seeketh knowledge” (Pro 18:15). Ecclesiastes then draws the line with a dryness that has never dated: “of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh” (Ecc 12:12). The one book a man is told to turn over day and night is the law of the LORD (Psa 1:2).

pos: n. (the Silesian duchy on the Olza, now Cieszyn; the one part of Silesia that kept a Lutheran majority through the Counter-Reformation)
etymology: From Polish Cieszyn, probably from a personal name Ciesz; germanised Teschen.
biblical_def: Teschen is the mountain duchy at the south-eastern corner of Silesia. It went Lutheran in the 1540s and stayed Lutheran in its people even after the Habsburgs took the duchy in 1653 and closed its churches. For nearly sixty years the Lutherans of Teschen had no legal church at all: they worshipped in houses, in the woods, and across the border in Hungary, and were served by preachers who came in illegally. In 1709, under the Convention of Altranstadt forced on the Emperor by Charles XII of Sweden, they were permitted one building outside the town walls — the Jesus Church, the only Protestant church left in Habsburg Silesia's south, which became the centre of Silesian Lutheranism and later of Silesian Pietism. The dictionary records Teschen for what endurance under loss actually looks like: “and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God” (Act 14:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tribulation as severe affliction, distresses of life, vexations; to spoil as to plunder, to strip by violence; and substance as that which is real, estate, means of living.
webster_full: TRIBULATION, n. [L. tribulo, to thresh.] Severe affliction; distresses of life; vexations; persecution for religion.
SPOIL, v.t. [L. spolio.] To plunder; to strip by violence; to rob; to take by violence from the owner.
SUBSTANCE, n. [L. substantia.] That which underlies all outward manifestation; estate; means of living; wealth.
PERSECUTION, n. The infliction of pain, punishment or death upon others unjustly, particularly for adhering to a religious creed.
ILLUMINATE, v.t. [L. illumino.] To enlighten; to adorn; to enlighten intellectually; to enlighten spiritually.
scriptures: Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.
Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.
But call to remembrance the former days, in which, after ye were illuminated, ye endured a great fight of afflictions;
For ye had compassion of me in my bonds, and took joyfully the spoiling of your goods, knowing in yourselves that ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance.
corruption_summary: The Silesian duchy on the Olza, now Cieszyn, whose Lutherans worshipped without a legal church for nearly sixty years until the Jesus Church was permitted in 1709.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a modern use of such histories that should be refused. Comfortable churches in free countries borrow the language of persecution for inconvenience and social disapproval, and the borrowing is cheapened by the real article. Teschen's Lutherans lost their buildings, their legal existence and in many cases their property, held services in forests, and smuggled in preachers at risk to both. The word persecution means that. It does not mean being disliked.

The principle to recover is that tribulation is the ordinary road rather than the exception. Paul does not console the young churches by promising relief; he tells them what the way is: “and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God” (Act 14:22), and states the rule without qualification — “Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” (2Ti 3:12). Hebrews recalls a congregation to its own earlier courage (Heb 10:32) and names what made the losses bearable: they “took joyfully the spoiling of your goods, knowing in yourselves that ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance” (Heb 10:34).

pos: n. (the Silesian fortress town on the Oder, now Glogow; forcibly re-Catholicised in 1628 and granted a Peace Church in 1652)
etymology: From Polish Glogow, from glog, the hawthorn; germanised Glogau.
biblical_def: Glogau was a Silesian ducal town and fortress on the Oder, Lutheran from early in the Reformation. In 1628, during the Thirty Years War, the Habsburg commissioners and Lichtenstein's dragoons came through Silesia closing Protestant churches and quartering soldiers in the houses of those who would not convert; Glogau's churches were taken and its Lutheran ministry expelled. At the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 the Emperor conceded three Friedenskirchen, peace churches, for the hereditary Silesian duchies — at Glogau, Jauer and Schweidnitz — to be built outside the walls, of wood and clay without nails, without towers or bells, within a year. The Glogau church was built and later burned; the Schweidnitz and Jauer churches still stand. The dictionary records the town for the terms on which the church was allowed to exist: “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a dragoon as a soldier who serves on horseback or on foot as occasion requires; to dragoon as to persecute by abandoning a place to the rage of soldiers; and a crown as a diadem, a reward of victory.
webster_full: DRAGOON, n. A soldier or musketeer who serves on horseback or on foot as occasion may require.
DRAGOON, v.t. To persecute by abandoning a place to the rage of soldiers; to compel to submit by violent measures.
CROWN, n. An ornament worn on the head by kings; a diadem; a reward of victory; honour, dignity.
SLAUGHTER, n. A killing; destruction of life by violence; carnage; butchery.
TRIBULATION, n. Severe affliction; distresses of life; persecution for religion.
scriptures: Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter.
Rom 8:36
As it is written, For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter.
Mat 5:10
Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
corruption_summary: The Silesian fortress town on the Oder, now Glogow; its Lutheran churches were seized in 1628 and a Peace Church outside the walls was conceded at Westphalia in 1652.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The honest reckoning is that the Peace Churches were a concession and a humiliation at once, and both halves get forgotten by turns. They were permitted only outside the walls, built without nails, forbidden towers or bells, and had to be finished within a year. Protestant accounts sometimes tell the story as a triumph of faith and leave out the terms; Catholic accounts cite the concession as tolerance and leave out the dragoons of 1628 that made it necessary. The dictionary records both halves.

The principle to recover is that the church's normal condition under a hostile power is survival on bad terms, and that Scripture promises a crown rather than a settlement. The letter to Smyrna does not predict relief; it fixes the duration and the duty: “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10). The Psalm says the slaughter is for God's sake and not a sign of his absence — “we are counted as sheep for the slaughter” (Psa 44:22) — and Paul quotes it in the middle of his argument that nothing can separate us from the love of Christ (Rom 8:36). The beatitude on the persecuted names the reason and the inheritance (Mat 5:10).

pos: n. (1562–1627; pastor at Fraustadt, who built a church in two stables and wrote a hymn in a plague year)
etymology: Herberger, a German surname from Herberge, an inn or lodging; Valerius, from Latin valere, to be strong.
biblical_def: Valerius Herberger was born at Fraustadt in Greater Poland, on the Silesian border, studied at Frankfurt an der Oder and Leipzig, and returned to his home town as schoolmaster and then as pastor. In 1604 the Catholic authorities took the parish church from the Lutheran congregation by royal order and locked them out. Herberger bought two houses beside the city gate, had their stables converted, and on Christmas Eve 1604 opened them as a church, calling it the Kripplein Christi, the little crib of Christ, because the Lord had been born in a stable before. He preached there for twenty-three years. In the plague of 1613 he stayed in the town and buried over two thousand of his people, and in that year wrote the hymn Valet will ich dir geben, a farewell to the world. The dictionary records him for the sign he took as his own: “and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn” (Luk 2:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a manger as a trough in which food is laid for cattle; a crib as the manger or rack of a stable; and a strait as a narrow pass, difficulty, distress.
webster_full: MANGER, n. A trough or box in which fodder is laid for cattle; the place in a stable where food is given.
CRIB, n. The manger or rack of a stable; a stall for oxen; a small habitation or cottage.
STRAIT, n. A narrow pass or passage; distress; difficulty; a condition of perplexity.
SWADDLE, v.t. To swathe; to bind as with a bandage; to bind tight with clothes.
DEPART, v.i. To go or move from; to leave; to die, to decease.
scriptures: Luk 2:7
And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.
Luk 2:12
And this shall be a sign unto you; Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger.
Php 1:23
For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better:
We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord.
corruption_summary: Pastor at Fraustadt who, locked out of his church in 1604, converted two stables into the Kripplein Christi; stayed through the plague of 1613 and wrote Valet will ich dir geben.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a sentimentality to resist, and Herberger himself would have resisted it. The Kripplein Christi makes a charming story — a congregation turned out of a stone church and worshipping in a stable at Christmas — and the charm obscures what it cost: a legal seizure the congregation could not reverse, two houses bought with their own money, and twenty-three years of worship in converted outbuildings. The name was a confession, not a decoration.

The principle to recover is that God's way of coming into the world was itself the pattern of refusal and humiliation, and that this is offered as the sign: “and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn” (Luk 2:7), and the angel gives it to the shepherds as the identifying mark — “Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger” (Luk 2:12). A pastor burying two thousand parishioners in one year is held between the two pulls Paul names: “having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better” (Php 1:23), and “willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord” (2Co 5:8).
